## Paper

## Abstract

Point defects critically govern the properties of two-dimensional semiconductors, yet their atomic-scale characteristics in the emerging MoSi N family remain unexplored. Here we combine atomic-resolution scanning transmission electron microscopy and first-principles calculations to systematically investigate point defects in monolayer semiconducting WSi N and MoSi N . We identify ten distinct defect types, with Si-for-top-N antisites (Si ), double-middle-N divacancies (V ), and double-top-N divacancies (V ) being the most abundant. These defects induce mobility modulation and bandgap reduction — in some cases leading to complete band closure and insulator-to-metal transitions — and, in certain configurations, give rise to spin-polarized bands with localized magnetic moments. Additionally, we observe low-dimensional assemblies formed via defect self-organization, including 2D Si networks and 1D Si2 chains. Our findings establish fundamental defect–property relationships and provide insights for defect-driven engineering of electronic and magnetic states in 2D WSi N and MoSi N semiconductors.

---

## Introduction

Point defects, which are ubiquitous in crystalline materials, have a significant influence on the electronic, optoelectronic, thermal, magnetic, and catalytic properties, particularly for 2D materials due to the reduced dimensionality1-14. Usually, point defects act as scattering centers of electrons and phonons, leading to a great degradation of electron mobility, thermal conductivity and photoelectric properties of 2D materials1,3,4,9,12,15-19. On the other hand, some unique or improved properties could be achieved by introducing point defects. For example, S vacancies in MoS can induce localized states, enabling MoS a carrier hopping transport phenomenon10; Pt vacancies in PtSe introduce localized magnetic moments, giving rise to the Kondo effect2; the Frenkel point defects and S vacancies greatly promote the hydrogen evolution reaction activity of monolayer MoS 6,11. Thus, understanding the point defects in 2D materials is essential not only for controlled growth of perfect crystals but also for tailoring their properties to meet various applications.

The MoSi N family is an emerging class of van der Waals (vdW) layered 2D materials with a sandwich-structured septuple-atomic-layer configuration20,21. Such unique structure enables MoSi N -like materials many interesting properties21-38, such as remarkable electrical, optical and valley-contrasting properties, piezoelectricity, ferroelectricity, magnetism, and catalytic properties. Meanwhile, the complex compositions and structures of the MoSi N family enable the formation of a wider variety of point defects compared to graphene, h-BN and transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs), providing greater degrees of freedom for tailoring the properties. Monolayer MoSi N and WSi N are the first two materials that have been synthesized by chemical vapor deposition (CVD) in the MoSi N family20,21.

Both of them are p-type 2D semiconductors with intrinsically higher carrier mobility, higher mechanical strength, higher thermal conductivity, and better stability than most 2D semiconductors20-22,39. Moreover, monolayer WSi N has been predicted to possess higher carrier mobilities and thermal conductivity than monolayer MoSi N 21,28. Although point defects have been predicted to have a significant influence on the properties of MoSi N -like materials38,40-43, the atomic structures of point defects remain experimentally unknown, leaving a critical gap in our understanding of their role in shaping material properties.

Here, we studied the point defects in monolayer MoSi N and WSi N using aberration-corrected scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) combined with first-principles calculations, with a focus on monolayer WSi N because it has higher tolerance to electron beam irradiation than MoSi N (Supplementary Figure 1). Four kinds of vacancies and six kinds of antisite substitutions were identified, among which the Si-for-top-N antisites (Si ), double-middle-N divacancies (V ), and double-top-N divacancies (V ) exhibited higher concentrations. First-principles calculations show that these point defects reduce the bandgap of monolayer WSi N : some completely close the bandgap, resulting in insulator-to-metal transition; some introduce spin-polarized bands, leading to local magnetic moments. Intriguingly, two low-dimensional defect configurations of 2D Si networks and 1D double-Si-for-Mo antisite (Si2 ) chains were identified in monolayer MoSi N , both exhibiting unique electronic characteristics.

---

## Results

Both WSi N and MoSi N monolayers were synthesized by CVD20. Atomic force microscopy (AFM) characterization of the MoSi N and WSi N samples transferred onto SiO substrates confirms their monolayer nature. The measured thicknesses are approximately 1.21 nm for MoSi N and 1.19 nm for WSi N (Supplementary Figure 2), which align with the reported values for monolayers20. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) characterization confirms the existence of W/Mo, Si, and N elements in WSi N /MoSi N (Supplementary Figures 3 and 4). It is worth noting that island-like multilayers can form under an increased NH flow. Such intentionally grown thick samples were used to reveal the cross-sectional atomic structure of WSi N .

Figure 1a and 1b are optical and bright-field TEM images of CVD-grown WSi N crystals, respectively, showing their triangular morphology. Figure 1c exhibits an annular dark field (ADF) - STEM image of monolayer WSi N , in which W and Si atoms are arranged into a projective hexagonal ring. Since Z-contrast ADF intensity is related to Z1.7 (Z, atomic number)44, W atoms are much brighter than Si atoms. To visualize the locations of N atoms, integrated differential phase contrast (iDPC) - STEM technique was adopted. As the intensity of iDPC-STEM image is approximately proportional to Z, the heavy and light elements can be captured simultaneously45. The iDPC-STEM image clearly demonstrates that the top N atoms are precisely positioned at the center of W-Si projective hexagonal rings (Fig. 1d). In contrast, the bilayer and trilayer WSi N display six-membered ring structures with distinct central features depending on the number of stacking layers (Supplementary Figure 5).

We have tried to acquire cross-sectional STEM images of monolayer WSi N . However, the inherent flexibility of monolayers led to severe bending and distortion during cross-sectional sample preparation, which prevented the resolution of atomic arrangements. Thus, we prepared multilayer WSi N samples to analyze the cross-sectional atomic structure of WSi N . As shown in Fig. 1e, the W, Si and N atoms form a septuple-atomic-layer configuration. The above STEM results confirm that WSi N has the same crystalline structure as the reported MoSi N monolayer20 (Supplementary Figure 6). Figure 1f presents the atomic schematic diagrams of monolayer WSi N , determined from the above characterizations.

Unlike single-atomic-layer graphene, WSi N exhibits a stereo structure with overlapped atoms of Si and N, increasing the difficulty of discerning point defect configurations. The structural determination of point defects requires the imaging of light N atoms, heavy W atoms, and Si atoms. However, iDPC-STEM is highly sensitive to variations in sample contaminants and image defocus46-49, which can introduce artifacts that may compromise the accuracy of structural analysis. Additionally, the lighter atoms result in a low signal-to-noise ratio in ADF-STEM imaging, especially when the materials contain heavier atoms50. Meanwhile, the local fluctuation of the sample also diminishes the accuracy of structural analysis for both ADF-STEM and iDPC-STEM50-56. Thus, we simultaneously employed iDPC- and ADF-STEM imaging, complemented by iDPC- and ADF-STEM simulations and first-principles calculations, to identify the point defects in monolayer WSi N .

Figures 2 and 3 show ten main point defect configurations that were observed in monolayer WSi N , including four vacancies and six antisite substitutions. The vacancies include V , V , double-Si-and-single-middle-N trivacancies (V ) and W vacancies (V ) (Fig. 2); the antisite substitutions include Si , Si-for-middle-N antisites (Si ), double-Si-for-W antisites (Si2 ), Si-for-W antisites (Si ), W-for-Si antisites (W ), and W-for-top-N antisites (W ) (Fig. 3). Notably, the ADF- and iDPC-STEM simulations of corresponding point defects are in good line with the experimental observations (Fig. 2a-d and Fig. 3a-d). Furthermore, the ADF line scan profiles across defective areas show good agreement between experimental and simulated images (Fig. 2e and Fig. 3e). These consistent results validate the reliability of our defect assignments. The obtained atomic models of point defects are presented in Fig. 2f and Fig. 3f. Similarly, identical point defects were observed in monolayer MoSi N , as shown in Supplementary Figures 7 and 8.

Notably, the absence of a single N atom in WSi N does not produce a detectable contrast change in the ADF and iDPC images, which prevented unambiguous identification of V and V (Supplementary Figure 9) and distinguishing the defect sets of V /V /V (Supplementary Figure 10) and V /V (Supplementary Figure 11). Moreover, due to the larger Z difference between W and Si/N, W exhibits similar contrast with W (Supplementary Figure 12). To identify these defects, we calculated the formation energies of various point defects by first-principles calculations under the experimentally determined Si-rich conditions (Fig. 4, Supplementary Figure 13, Supplementary Table 1 and see Supplementary Note 1 for calculation details). The obtained formation energies follow the trend V < V < V , V < V , and W < W (Supplementary Figure 14). Thus, we assign these defects as V , V , and W , rather than V (V ), V , and W , respectively. It is worth noting that adatoms are highly mobile under electron beam irradiation and thus are relatively straightforward to be distinguished compared to lattice defects.

Figures 4a and 4b show large field-of-view STEM images of monolayer WSi N , clearly demonstrating the diversity of point defect structures present within a single sample. We then counted the concentration of the ten kinds of point defects by statistically analyzing 140 atomic-resolution STEM images, encompassing 6600 defects. As shown in Fig. 4c, the most prevalent defects are Si , V , and V . This is in sharp contrast to CVD-grown MoS monolayers, where only sulfur vacancy (V ) was frequently detected9,57. The frequent occurrence of multiple types of point defects in WSi N , including vacancies and antisite substitutions, reveals its inherently more complex structural configuration. The Si antisite and V vacancy exhibit the highest defect concentrations ‒ (2.12 ± 0.002) × 1013 cm-2 and (1.14 ± 0.005) × 1013 cm-2, respectively ‒ which are comparable to that of V in CVD-grown MoS (1.2 × 1013 cm-2)9. In contrast, the concentrations of other defects, such as V and V are much lower. It should be noted that the statistical analysis of V may inadvertently include V and V due to their nearly identical image contrast, even though V configuration is thermodynamically most stable and dominant. This leads to a potential overestimation of the true V concentration. Similarly, the statistical analysis of W possibly includes the case of W .

Furthermore, it should be noted that W-containing vacancy complexes do exist. For instance, Supplementary Figure 15 shows the absence of two Si atoms and two N(t) atoms around the missing W atom. Owing to the multiple atomic configurations of W-containing vacancy complexes and their inherently low concentration, all instances were included in the statistical analysis of V . For simplicity, the term tungsten vacancies (V ) was used representatively to present the statistical results.

To understand the formation of the observed defects, we first conducted in-situ STEM experiments at 300 kV to rule out the influence of electron beam irradiation. During the observation for normal photography with only one brief irradiation event, no new point defects were formed. After ~33 s STEM image preview, only a limited number of new nitrogen vacancies emerged (Supplementary Figure 16), along with the migration of a few tungsten adatoms. Continued exposure of 102 s led to occasional ejection of W atoms from the lattice at a few sites (Supplementary Figure 17). Furthermore, electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) confirmed the absence of O in the WSi N (Supplementary Figure 18). These results collectively demonstrate the robust stability of monolayer WSi N under STEM imaging. Moreover, in our experiments, we frequently moved the sample to different locations. Each position was subjected to no more than 5 s preview and only one image acquisition. Therefore, the observed defects intrinsically originate from the CVD growth process rather than being caused by electron beam irradiation.

Furthermore, we systematically evaluated the stability of point defects in monolayer WSi N under various experimental conditions. First, defect concentration statistics remained consistent at different STEM beam currents (~5–20 pA), with minor variations attributable to sample heterogeneity (Supplementary Figure 19 and Supplementary Table 2). Second, defects showed no measurable change after two months of ambient exposure (Supplementary Figure 20). Third, electrical biasing at 1 V induced no detectable alteration in defect types or concentrations (Supplementary Figure 21). Finally, thermal cycling up to 500 °C likewise preserved the defect configurations (Supplementary Figure 22). Collectively, these results confirm that the identified point defects are structurally and chemically stable under the employed imaging conditions, upon ambient exposure, as well as under moderate electrical and thermal stress.

As shown in Fig. 1f, monolayer WSi N consists of seven elementally distinct atomic layers. The formation of point defects during its growth is highly sensitive to CVD atmosphere. In our experiments, a quartz tube served as Si source, creating a Si-rich environment. Meanwhile, the supply of N was limited because a higher NH flow rate would cause undesirable etching of the Cu growth substrate. Under such Si-rich and N-deficient environments, the formation of Si substitute defects and N vacancies is thermodynamically favored. This is because excess silicon can substitute atoms in various layers while maintaining coordination symmetry, and N deficiency promotes vacancy formation across all four N layers. Experimentally, the dominant point defects observed include antisites (e.g., Si , Si , Si2 , and Si ) and vacancy complexes (e.g., V and V ), consistent with these expectations. The increasing concentration of Si and Si2 defects with higher Si supply (Supplementary Figure 23) further supports the preliminary understanding on the formation mechanism of defects.

Moreover, the observed point defect concentrations correlate with their calculated formation energies (Fig. 4c). In WSi N , the formation energies of vacancies are generally higher than those of antisite substitutions, similar to the case of MoSi N 43. Thus, antisite substitutions are more frequently observed in comparison with vacancies. This is in sharp contrast to the case of MoS , where vacancies are generally more stable than antisite substitutions9,57. Notably, the concentration of V and V are relatively high despite their higher formation energy, even surpassing that of antisite substitutions with lower formation energy. Two primary factors may account for this observation. First, the formation energies of single V and V vacancies (3.89 eV and 3.21 eV, respectively) are approximately half those of their double-vacancy counterparts, V and V (8.31 eV and 6.18 eV). This near-additivity behavior suggests weak coupling between the two single vacancies in V and V . Consequently, a high concentration of single vacancies could facilitate the formation of double vacancies through statistical pairing. Second, the N(t) atoms at the outermost surface are more susceptible to damage during TEM sample preparation, including transfer and heat treatment. It is worth noting that once a V forms near an N(m) atom, the computed energy barrier for N(m) moving towards the adjacent V is relatively low compared to that for W or Si escaping into the vacuum (Supplementary Figure 24). This suggests that N(m) atoms are susceptible to environmental disturbances in the presence of N(t) vacancies, which may further contribute to an increased concentration of V defects.

In certain cases, a discrepancy arises between the experimentally derived defect concentration and the corresponding calculated formation energy, such as the case of W . There are several reasons for such discrepancy. First, the formation energies of point defects are strongly influenced by chemical potential, which may differ between experimental and calculation conditions58. Second, our computational modeling was confined to point defects within a 4 × 4 × 1 supercell (already large for the DFT calculations), which corresponds to an unrealistically high defect concentration (~ 0.74 nm-2) compared to the much lower experimental concentration (~0.01 nm-2). Third, our calculations assume charge-neutral defects, but the possibility of charged defects cannot be excluded58. Fourth, while we assume defect-induced charge distribution is delocalized across the lattice, the potential impact of charge localization on formation energy remains difficult to rule out58.

We then conducted first-principles spin-polarized density functional theory (DFT) calculations to explore the influence of the observed point defects on the electronic properties of monolayer WSi N (Fig. 5, Supplementary Table 1). Pristine monolayer WSi N is a 2D semiconductor with an indirect bandgap of 2.09 eV. The presence of point defects reduces the bandgaps to 0.64 ‒ 1.26 eV depending on the types of point defects. The presence of V , Si2 , W , and W defects induces a change in the bandgap type from indirect to direct. Notably, the introduction of V , V , Si , Si , and Si defects completely closes the bandgap, resulting in insulator-to-metal transitions. Additionally, V , V , V , V , W , and W defects introduce spin-polarized bands, leading to local magnetic moments. For vacancies, the magnetic moment in V originates from the three surrounding W atoms; similarly, the magnetic moment in V arises from the three N(t) atoms on the upper and lower surfaces; V has a magnetic moment of 0.51 μ , which is attributed to the three surrounding Si atoms; V has a magnetic moment of 1.02 μ , which stems from the three Si atoms on the upper and lower surfaces. Notably, the magnetic moment of V is twice that of V , indicating the weak coupling effect between the two aligned N(t) atoms. For antisite substitutions, W and W exhibit magnetism derived from the antisite W atoms. Particularly, W possesses the largest magnetic moment of 2.11μ among all the point defects.

We further calculated the orbital-resolved density of states (DOSs) to identify the orbital characters of in-gap states (Supplementary Figure 25). The contribution from vacancies was obtained by introducing pseudo atoms into the positions of vacancies. It is found that for V , V , V , Si , Si2 , and Si , the in-gap states are predominantly composed of W orbitals. While for V and V , the in-gap states are primarily composed of Si orbitals. For W and W , the in-gap states are mainly attributed to the defect orbitals. These in-gap states induced by point defects strongly modulate the electronic and magnetic structure of pristine WSi N (Fig. 5, Supplementary Table 1) and therefore change the associated optical properties. For instance, the presence of V decreases the bandgap by inducing the in-gap states, which introduce additional optical absorption within the bandgap (Supplementary Figure 26). In particular, these in-gap states are rather localized, which is manifested by the appearance of flat bands within the bandgap (Fig. 5). These flat bands significantly increase the hole effective mass at  from 1.5m (pristine) to 15.3 m and thus decrease the hole mobility from 411 cm2s-1V-1 (pristine) to 2 cm2s-1V-1 according to the deformation potential theory9,59. In contrast, the introduction of Si reduces the Fermi energy, resulting in an almost rigid upward shift of the band structure and triggering an insulator-to-metal transition (Fig. 5). The crossing of the maximum valence band with the Fermi energy facilitates optical transitions within the infrared regime (Supplementary Figure 26). Furthermore, the presence of Si significantly increases hole mobility, reaching a value of 740 cm2s-1V-1.

To correlate the theoretical calculation results, we used atomic-scale scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) to probe the impact of point defects on the local electronic structure of monolayer WSi N . The surface tunneling properties of STM allowed us to identify V and Si defects from topographic images (Fig. 6). Scanning tunneling spectroscopy (STS) measurements on a defect-free region (Figs. 6a, b) revealed a bandgap of ~2.05 eV, consistent with our DFT prediction (2.09 eV). In contrast, STS on defect sites showed significantly reduced bandgaps (Figs. 6c, d), with values approaching the calculated gap (0.84 eV) for V defects. The discrepancy between the easy identification of V by STM and its limited representation in STEM images is due to the distinct imaging mechanisms and sensitivities of the two techniques. An additional defect site exhibited a metallic signature, which we identify as the Si defect—consistent with our theoretical prediction of its metallic character. These results confirm the decisive influence of point defects on the electronic properties of WSi N .

We further measured the ultraviolet and visible (UV-Vis) absorption spectra of three distinct WSi N samples and obtained their corresponding Tauc plots (Supplementary Figure 27): the original sample, the sample annealed in Ar at 300 °C for 12 h, and the sample annealed in air at 300 °C for 12 h. The absorption data showed similar bandgaps for the original sample (~2.1 eV) and the air-annealed sample (~2 eV), indicating that the point defects exhibit oxidation resistance in air at the evaluated temperature. In contrast, the sample annealed in Ar exhibited a noticeable reduced bandgap of ~1.8 eV, indicating an increase in defect concentration. In our work, the annealed samples were used to obtain high-quality STEM images for defect concentration analysis. Taking the V defect as example, argon annealing led to a significantly higher defect concentration compared to air annealing (Supplementary Figure 28), consistent with the more pronounced bandgap reduction.

The comprehensive atomic-scale catalog of point defects in monolayer WSi N , together with their tunable properties, offer significant opportunities for device engineering. For example, the substantially increased hole mobility by Si defect suggests its utility for channel optimization. Defects that induce an insulator-to-metal transition, such as V , Si , Si , and Si , when strategically incorporated at contact interfaces, may lower the Schottky barrier height, reduce contact resistance, and enhance on-state current density. Similarly, the Si antisite defects introduce a shallow acceptor state near the valence band maximum, enabling effective p-type doping for threshold voltage tuning. Conversely, in-gap states induced by V defects promote trap-assisted tunneling, potentially increasing the off-state leakage current and reducing the switching ratio. Consequently, optimizing field effect transistor performance—balancing high mobility, low leakage, and low contact resistance—will require precise spatial defect engineering: suppressing channel-degrading defects, leveraging mobility-enhancing defects in the active region, and potentially incorporating beneficial defects at contact interfaces.

Furthermore, although pristine WSi N exhibits high intrinsic thermal conductivity, a trait well-suited for transistor applications, high concentrations of defects such as V and Si are expected to substantially reduce the lattice thermal conductivity through mass-contrast and strain-field scattering, as observed in other 2D systems60-62. Such reduction is highly advantageous for thermoelectric applications, where a lowered lattice thermal conductivity directly enhances the thermoelectric figure of merit ZT, particularly when coupled with defect-tuned electronic properties, for example, the metallic states introduced by Si defects.

Beyond isolated point defects in monolayer WSi N and MoSi N , we observe a propensity for defect aggregation in these materials. Figures 7a-c and Supplementary Figure 29 exhibit typical ADF images of double, triple, and multiple Si aggregations in MoSi N and WSi N monolayers, respectively. It is worth noting that Si could even form a 2D network in certain areas of MoSi N monolayer (Fig. 7c). Simulated ADF images of Si networks are in accordance with the experimental observations (Fig. 7d). Geometric phase analysis (GPA) analysis indicates the absence of lattice strain across the Si 2D networks and MoSi N matrixes (Supplementary Figure 30). Structurally, the Si 2D network is a periodic, planar crystalline defect characterized by the aggregation of collective Si antisite defects on one side of the MoSi N monolayer, analogous to a stacking fault.

Taking MoSi N as an example, we constructed defect aggregation models containing one, two, and three Si defects within a 4 × 4 × 1 configuration of the MoSi N unit cell (Supplementary Figures 31 and 32) and calculated their corresponding binding energies. The configurations with Si antisite defects aggregated on one side of the monolayer MoSi N exhibit higher stability (Supplementary Figure 33). The increased binding energies with the quantity of Si located on one side suggest that Si defect aggregation is energetically favorable (Supplementary Figures 33 and 34). Moreover, the formation of 2D Si network triggers electronic structure reconstruction in the MoSi N system (Fig. 7e). Similar to isolated Si point defects43, the introduction of 2D Si network induces bandgap closure. Systematic analysis of DOSs demonstrates that the electronic states near the Fermi level in 2D Si network are predominantly contributed by the 3p orbitals of Si atoms (Fig. 7f).

Additionally, we observed a 1D point defect chain embedded in monolayer MoSi N (Fig. 7g), where no lattice strain was detected as well (Supplementary Figure 35). Careful examination of defect configurations in an enlarged ADF-STEM image revealed a 1D Si2 chain (Fig. 7h), in good agreement with corresponding ADF image simulation (Fig. 7i). This Si2 chain is a linear crystalline defect that separates the single-crystal MoSi N monolayer into two parts without a misorientation angle, analogous to a 0° grain boundary in 2D materials. We constructed the 1D chain-like models containing one, two, three and four Si2 within a 4 × 4 × 1 configuration of the MoSi N unit cell (Supplementary Figure 36) and calculated their binding energies. Similar to the 2D Si aggregations, the binding energies of these 1D defect aggregations increase as the quantity of Si2 increases (Supplementary Figure 37), indicating the increasing energetical stability for linear assembly of Si2 . Upon introducing this 1D chain into MoSi N , the bandgap of the system significantly decreases from 1.72 eV to 0.40 eV (Fig. 7j). Further DOSs analysis reveals that the 1D chain-induced in-gap states near the Fermi level are dominated by the d-orbitals of Mo atoms (Fig. 7k).

The thermodynamic stability of the observed 2D Si networks and 1D Si2 chains, as confirmed by our binding‑energy calculations, is consistent with an in‑situ assembly mechanism during CVD growth rather than post‑growth migration. The high‑temperature growth environment provides sufficient atomic mobility and a concurrent supply of all constituent elements, allowing direct incorporation of multi‑site defects into the extending lattice. The seamless embedding and crystallographic alignment of these extended structures further indicate a growth‑governed process. First‑principles migration‑barrier calculations additionally show that post‑growth rearrangement of isolated Si or Si2 defects—even in the presence of nearby vacancies—requires overcoming high energy barriers (> 4 eV) (Supplementary Figure 38), rendering large‑scale diffusion kinetically unfeasible under ambient conditions. Collectively, the structural coherence, energetic trends, and calculated kinetic barriers support a kinetically enabled, growth‑mediated pathway for the formation of these low‑dimensional defect aggregates.

In summary, by combining atomic-resolution STEM imaging and first-principles calculations, we revealed point defect configurations in monolayer semiconductors WSi N and MoSi N and their influence on material properties. Ten distinct types of lattice point defects, comprising four vacancies and six antisite substitutions, were identified. Taking monolayer WSi N as a representative system, we demonstrated that these defects substantially modulate electronic structure, induce magnetism, and alter optical responses. Furthermore, we identified two defect aggregation configurations in monolayer MoSi N : 2D Si networks and 1D Si2 chains, which exhibit significant influence on the electronic band structure. This work provides crucial insights into the defect-property correlation of monolayer semiconducting WSi N and MoSi N , which is essential for controlled synthesis and property engineering of such materials and paves the way for their applications in nanoelectronics, spintronics, and catalytic systems.

---

## Methods

Sample preparation
The monolayer WSi N and MoSi N samples were first grown on Cu/W and Cu/Mo substrates, respectively, by CVD method20. Then, they were transferred onto the TEM grids coated with silicon nitrogen membranes by the chemical etching method with the help of a polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) layer. After that, the TEM grids were immersed in hot acetone to dissolve the PMMA layer and subsequently annealed at 300 ℃ for 12 hours in air to remove hydrocarbon residues from the sample surfaces before inserting them into the electron microscope.

Structural characterization and simulation
The optical microscopy image was obtained on Nikon LV100D. The thicknesses of samples were measured using an atomic force microscope (AFM, MultiMode 8, Bruker, Inc.). Optical absorption spectra were recorded using an ultraviolet and visible spectrophotometry (UV-Vis, JASCO V-770). The BF-TEM image was obtained on a FEI Tecnai F20 at 200kV. The ADF- and iDPC-STEM imaging of monolayer WSi N and MoSi N was performed on a FEI Titan Cube Themis G2 300 instrument equipped with a high-brightness field-emission gun (X-FEG), double spherical aberration corrector and a monochromator. The accelerating voltage was 300 kV. For imaging the lattice point defects, the camera length was 230 mm; the collection semi-angle was 25 - 152 mrad for ADF imaging, while 6 - 24 mrad for iDPC imaging; the major beam current was set to ~ 9 pA. The STEM image acquisition and preview were typically conducted under the conditions of 5 μs dwell time with 2048  2048 pixels and 1.32  107 e- nm-2 electron dose and 1 μs dwell time with 1024  1024 pixels and 6.6×105 e- nm-2 electron dose, respectively. For imaging the Si 2D network and Si2 1D chain in MoSi N , the camera length was 145 mm; the collection semi-angle was 37 - 200 mrad for ADF imaging; the beam current was set to ~ 22 pA.

To ensure image quality, annealing treatment was carried out for all samples to remove surface contaminants as thoroughly as possible before STEM imaging. To improve the image contrast and signal-to-noise ratio of Si substitutions in the 2D networks and 1D chains, we selected strictly flat zones in monolayer MoSi N samples and extended the image exposure time to 10 μs dwell time with 2048 × 2048 pixels. The stability comparison for monolayer WSi N and MoSi N was conducted on JEOL ARM 200F at 200 kV.

The ADF- and iDPC-STEM images were simulated using ToTEM63 or Dr. Probe64 software based on multi-slice method. The simulation parameters were in accordance with the experimental values, disregarding any aberrations. The atomic models were optimized by DFT. To compensate for structural distortions (elongation or compression) in experimental images caused by sample drift, equivalent deformations were intentionally introduced into the simulated images to achieve precise atom-to-atom alignment.

For the statistical analysis of defect concentration, we acquired a large number of STEM images – each with a typical area of 9.45 × 9.45 nm2 – from random locations across multiple WSi N samples. The types of point defects were identified by combining STEM image contrast (ADF and iDPC) with image simulations. For V and Si point defects with inherently relatively high concentration, we used CalAtom software to perform the high-throughput statistical analysis65. The defect positions were identified by analyzing the intensity variations in ADF images. Other types of point defects were directly counted manually due to the limited quantity. The defect concentration was determined by normalizing the number of defects to the corresponding imaging area. Due to the low concentration, the datasets for V and V defects exhibited a discrete distribution. Therefore, a weighted averaging method was used to estimate their concentrations. For other defects, to minimize experimental statistical errors, Gaussian fitting was applied to the datasets to obtain the mean (μ) and variance (σ), yielding the final concentration values (Supplementary Figure 39).

For the biasing- and heating-STEM experiments, an in-situ thermoelectric holder (Protochips inc.) was used. Biasing was performed in constant voltage mode using a four-probe electrical chip, with the voltage increased to 1 V in steps of 0.1 V/s. Heating was conducted with a two-probe thermal chip, where temperature was raised from 25 °C to 500 °C at a ramp rate of 0.5 °C/s. The thermal cycling procedure comprised three stages: (1) heating to 500 °C for ∼1 h, (2) cooling to room temperature for ∼0.5 h, and (3) reheating to 500 °C for ∼1 h.

STM measurements
The monolayer WSi N sample was initially introduced into a combined scanning tunneling microscope–molecular beam epitaxy (STM-MBE) system (Unisoku Co., USM1500) and annealed at ~300 °C for 12 hours under ultrahigh vacuum to achieve an atomically clean surface. The base pressure during annealing was maintained at 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ Torr. After annealing, the sample was transferred to a low-temperature STM stage without breaking the vacuum. All the STM and STS experiments were conducted at liquid nitrogen temperature (~78 K). The STM topographic images were acquired under the constant-current mode using a PtIr tip, while the STS spectra were collected via a lock-in amplification technique with an AC modulation of 60 mV at a frequency of 879 Hz.

Theoretical calculations
First-principles calculations were carried out using the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package66,67. The generalized gradient approximation of Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof68 was used for the exchange-correlation functional. The interaction between nuclei and valence electrons was described by the pseudopotential within the framework of the projector augmented wave method69. The plane wave cutoff was set to 450 eV. To model the point defects, a supercell slab of 4 × 4 × 1 unit cell with a vacuum width of 20 Å was employed. The electronic optimization was performed until the total energy difference between two iterations was less than 10-6 eV. The structural relaxation was terminated until the force on each atom was smaller than 0.01 eV/Å. More computational details on the calculations of defect formation energy and binding energy are provided in Supplementary Note 1.

### Reviewer 1

Response to reviewers’ comments
We sincerely appreciate the reviewers’ insightful comments and constructive
suggestions, which have helped us significantly improve the quality and clarity of our
work. Below, we provide a point-by-point response to each reviewer’s concerns. All
revisions in the manuscript are highlighted in blue for easy reference.
Reviewer 1

### Reviewer 3

Tong et al present a study of point defects in WSi2N4 and MoSi2N4 using scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) and complementary density functional theory (DFT) . There is certainly value in such an imaging and DFT study and I recognise that the imaging of such systems may be challenging, especially if they are electron beam sensitive (although the sensitivity of the materials is not discussed in the manuscript except to qualitatively state without experimental evidence that WSi2N4 is more stable than MoSi2N4). The work presents several interesting observations that will be of interest to those exploiting the properties of this relatively new class of materials. However, there are several areas where I feel clarification and improvement to the STEM data analysis presented is required before publication in Nature Comms could be recommended.
The authors explain that simultaneous iDPC and ADF imaging modes are required to give confidence in the presence of the different defects being observed. However, their simulations are only for the ADF image mode. It is essential that the comparison is made with STEM image simulations of both iDPC and ADF images. The authors compare line scans for the simulations of defective material to line scans from the simulations of the pristine system, but they also need to directly compare line scans to equivalent line scans from the experimental data, to give confidence in the assignment of different defects and subsequent analysis. Especially, in Figure 2 the assignment of the point defects of the VN(m)2, VN(t)2 and SiN2 is not convincingly shown.
Also for the VW image in Figure 2 the neighboring Si columns in the experimental data do not appear to be in the same position as they are in the simulation. Were the simulations performed on DFT relaxed xyz structure files or simply by removing the vacancy atom from the lattice? Simulations should be performed on the DFT relaxed structures. If the former relaxed DFT models are already used, possibly this VW vacancy could be a larger defect than just a single W vacancy?
In Figure S2 it is difficult to assess the confidence of the defect assignment as even the ADF simulations are not shown alongside the experimental data. The authors should also further explain why the atoms are assumed to be substitutional point defects rather than adatoms on the surface (due to knock on damage from the electron beam). I agree that there is clearly a long defect line where W atoms are missing, visible in Figure 5g,h,i. However, I do not think that the assignment of SiN(t) locations and agglomerations in Figure 5a-c (and SI Figure S11) is sufficiently convincingly demonstrated. I also do not thing that the term “superstructure” is justified given the disorder and inconsistency of the assignment of defects.
The scale of the sets of images in Figure 2 and FigureS2 are also not presented with an identical scale and the scales of the experiments does not always match the simulations, which does not help with the comparison and is distracting.
The imaging presented here is performed at 300 kV so the defects are likely to be overwhelmingly electron beam induced. At such an accelerating voltage, knock-on damage is likely to be dominant and N is likely to be more susceptible to knock on damage than Si and Si. The authors need to consider the knock on damage cross sections of the different atomic species when interpreting their defect results. They should also explain why 300 kV was chosen over an accelerating voltage of 80kV which is commonly recommended for reducing defect creation when imaging transition metal dichalcogenides.
Given the complexity and ambiguity of several of their defect assignments, the manuscript lacks sufficient evidence to support the experimental evidence of defect population data in Figure 3. The authors need to show evidence of examples of labelling of defects over large STEM fields of view, a statistical analysis of the defect concentration as a function of total electron fluence and a clear statement of the number of each type of defect that was identified. Where several possible defect types have been combined in the histogram or where it is not possible to detect a particular defect type due to insufficient signal to noise ratio this should be noted more clearly in the figure caption.
The authors should also demonstrate how they know the materials are monolayer by comparing to image simulations for bilayer and thicker materials. Figure S2 shows many bright atoms around the defects that are circled. These should be discussed. Are these Mo or W impurity adatoms?
The atomic models of the point defects should be shown more clearly and not only as tiny covering up part of the experimental images. If the authors feel there is not space in the main text figures, they can be shown clearly and from several different crystallographic directions angles in the SI. I also so not understand why some of the ADF panels (in Figure 5a-c and examples in SI) are presented on a red colour look up table. I did not find it helped to follow the assignment of defect types in these images.

Q4: Given the high theoretical thermal conductivity of pristine WSi₂N₄ and the established role of point defects as potent phonon scatterers, the observed high concentrations of defects (e.g., VN(m)², SiN(t)) are likely to significantly suppress lattice thermal transport. To broaden the impact of this work into the realms of thermal management and thermoelectrics, we suggest the authors include an estimate or a brief discussion on this effect.
Q5: This work provides a superb atomic-scale catalog of defects and their electronic signatures. To maximize its impact, the manuscript would benefit from a forward-looking discussion on the potential device-level implications. For instance, how might the prevalent defects influence key metrics in a prototypical WSi₂N₄ field-effect transistor (e.g., contact resistance, leakage current)?
Q6: For practical applications in electronics or spintronics, it is crucial to understand how these defects behave under ambient exposure (moisture/oxygen), electrical bias, or thermal cycling. Do the charge states of electrically active defects (e.g., SiN(t)) remain stable under gate voltage? Could the observed N vacancies act as degradation sites during device operation? A discussion on these aspects would bridge the gap between fundamental defect characterization and realistic device reliability considerations.

### Reviewer 2

All the concerns raised have been well addressed, and the text and figures are now organized much better, before the manuscript to be published, only a few minor points need to clarify:
1. In Fig.6cd, the STS of the defects 2-4 look almost the same line shape, there are remarkably two electronic states at 1eV, close to the conduction band edge. the author assign this defect as V_N(t), and the STM image also shows this defect is abundant, however this defect is not common according to the statistical results in Fig.4 c. the assignment of Si_N(t) is reasonable, as it has high concentration in STEM image analysis and its STS shows it is metallic.
2. The defect 4 (purple arrow) and defect 2 (blue arrow) give different contrast in the STM image in Fig. 6c, but they correspond to the same defect, please explain why or remove some of the arrows to avoid misunderstanding, since the defect assignment in STM is quite difficult and heavily depends on the experience.

### Reviewer 3

The authors have added additional simulations, analysed a larger data volume and added STM data which has improved their manuscript. I now recommend it for publication. It is unfortunate that the authors do not plan to include the image data uploaded to a free repository for the field to benefit from and I recommend they consider doing this.
